title: Reproducibility becomes part of the job

blocks.text: Repeatable processing offered more than speed. It could make a method inspectable. A script, SQL query, graphical model, workspace or configuration file can preserve the logic used to create an output. If the same inputs and parameters remain available, another practitioner has a better chance of rerunning the work than if the method survives only as a remembered sequence of menu choices. National datasets and operational services may need to be rebuilt regularly, so the method itself becomes part of the production record.

blocks.text: Reproducibility required documented inputs, dependencies and processing steps. The software version may change, a library may disappear, a web service may alter its response, or a source dataset may gain a new field while losing an old one. Paths, credentials and environment settings can be as important as the visible processing logic. A workflow that depends on “C:\GIS\Final\Final2\ReallyFinal” is still automation, but it is not yet much of an institutional asset.

blocks.text: Version control brought software-development practice closer to GIS production. By the 2020s some spatial teams were managing scripts, configuration and even geographic change histories through repository-style tools. LINZ’s use of Kart in the Future Topographic Maps programme is a particularly direct example because the organisation describes it as spatial version control. Version control makes changes traceable, comparable and recoverable as the production dataset evolves.
